instructions: Chapter-wise questions from ICSE board, compartment and specimen papers, 2015–2024.

questions.chapter: Object-Oriented Programming Concepts
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a feature of Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) implemented by classes in Java?

options.c: Encapsulation
options.d: Compilation

questions.solution: (d) Compilation. Compilation is a step in running a program, not an OOP feature; abstraction, inheritance and encapsulation are.

questions.chapter: Values, Data Types and Operators
questions.question: What is the size of an int data type in Java?

options.c: 4 bytes
options.d: 8 bytes

questions.solution: (c) 4 bytes. An int occupies 32 bits = 4 bytes in Java.

questions.chapter: Encapsulation
questions.question: What is the primary purpose of encapsulation in Java?

options.b: To hide the implementation details and protect data
options.c: To provide faster compilation
options.d: To improve runtime efficiency

questions.solution: (b) To hide the implementation details and protect data. Encapsulation wraps data and methods together and restricts direct access to the data.

questions.chapter: Class as the Basis of Computation
questions.question: A class is called :

options.c: Composite data type
options.d: All of these

questions.solution: (d) All of these. A class creates many objects (object factory), is defined by the programmer (user-defined type) and groups several members of different types (composite type).

questions.chapter: Class as the Basis of Computation
questions.question: A variable whose value is not associated to an object and its value exists throughout the life of the program is a?

options.c: Final variable
options.d: None of these

questions.solution: (b) Static variable. A static variable belongs to the class, not to any object, and lives as long as the program runs.

questions.chapter: Class as the Basis of Computation
questions.topic: Object name in a creation statement
questions.question:
In the below statement, what is the name of the object being created?
Student stu = new Student();

options.c: Stu
options.d: None of these

questions.solution: (b) stu. Student is the class; stu is the object (reference variable). Java is case-sensitive, so Stu is different.

questions.chapter: Class as the Basis of Computation

options.c: name, x
options.d: age, p

questions.solution: (a) name, age. Data members are declared inside the class but outside every method; x and p are local variables of main().

questions.chapter: Values, Data Types and Operators
questions.question: For which of the following data types, the size of the variable declared will be fixed?

options.c: Composite
options.d: None of these

questions.solution: (a) Primitive. Every primitive type has a fixed size (e.g. int 4 bytes, double 8 bytes); the size of composite/reference data depends on its members.

questions.chapter: Object-Oriented Programming Concepts
questions.topic: OOP characteristic implemented by a class
questions.question: A class implements which of the following Object Oriented programming characteristic?

options.c: Abstraction
options.d: Polymorphism

questions.solution: (a) Encapsulation. A class wraps data members and member methods into a single unit, which is encapsulation.

questions.chapter: Class as the Basis of Computation
questions.question: The messages are passed in a class using :

options.c: Objects
options.d: None of these

questions.solution: (b) Function parameters. A message is a method call; the data it carries is passed through the method's parameters.

questions.chapter: Class as the Basis of Computation
questions.question:
Statement 1 : The new operator in Java is used to create objects dynamically at runtime.
Statement 2 : The new operator is also responsible for deleting objects from memory when they are no longer used.

options.c: Statement 1 is true, but Statement 2 is false.
options.d: Statement 1 is false, but Statement 2 is true.

questions.solution: (c) Statement 1 is true, but Statement 2 is false. new allocates memory for objects at runtime; unused objects are removed by Java's garbage collector, not by new.

questions.chapter: Class as the Basis of Computation
questions.topic: Objects as instances of a class
questions.question:
Statement 1 : An object is an instance of a class and can have its own unique state and behavior.
Statement 2 : A class can only have one object created from it.

options.c: Statement 1 is true, but Statement 2 is false.
options.d: Statement 1 is false, but Statement 2 is true.

questions.solution: (c) Statement 1 is true, but Statement 2 is false. A class is an object factory: any number of objects can be created from it.

questions.chapter: Class as the Basis of Computation
questions.topic: Lifetime of local and instance variables
questions.question:
Statement 1 : In Java, local variables are destroyed once the method or block in which they are defined finishes execution.
Statement 2 : Instance variables are tied to specific objects and their lifetime depends on the object.

options.c: Statement 1 is true, but Statement 2 is false.
options.d: Statement 1 is false, but Statement 2 is true.

questions.solution: (a) Both statements are true. Local variables exist only while their block runs; each object has its own copy of the instance variables, which lives as long as the object.

questions.chapter: Encapsulation
questions.question:
Statement 1 : The public access specifier makes class members accessible from anywhere in the program.
Statement 2 : The private access specifier makes class members accessible from subclasses of the class.

options.c: Statement 1 is true, but Statement 2 is false.
options.d: Statement 1 is false, but Statement 2 is true.

questions.solution: (c) Statement 1 is true, but Statement 2 is false. private members are accessible only inside their own class, not in subclasses.

questions.chapter: Class as the Basis of Computation
questions.question:
Statement 1 : A class is a blueprint for creating objects.
Statement 2 : A variable of a primitive type can also act as an object.

options.c: Statement 1 is true, but Statement 2 is false.
options.d: Statement 1 is false, but Statement 2 is true.

questions.solution: (c) Statement 1 is true, but Statement 2 is false. Primitive variables (int, char, boolean...) hold plain values and are not objects.

questions.chapter: Values, Data Types and Operators
questions.question:
Statement 1 : In Java, variables declared with the final keyword cannot be reassigned after their initial assignment.
Statement 2 : The final keyword can also be used to prevent a class from being subclassed.

options.c: Statement 1 is true, but Statement 2 is false.
options.d: Statement 1 is false, but Statement 2 is true.

questions.solution: (a) Both statements are true. A final variable is a constant, and a final class cannot be extended.

questions.chapter: Class as the Basis of Computation
questions.topic: State, behaviour and class of an object
questions.question:
Statement 1 : An object's state is defined by its attributes, while its behavior is defined by its methods.
Statement 2 : An object in Java can exist without being associated with a class.

options.c: Statement 1 is true, but Statement 2 is false.
options.d: Statement 1 is false, but Statement 2 is true.

questions.solution: (c) Statement 1 is true, but Statement 2 is false. Every Java object is created from a class, its blueprint.

questions.chapter: Values, Data Types and Operators
questions.question:
Statement 1 : Composite data types in Java can combine different types of data into a single entity.
Statement 2 : Primitive data types like int and float are examples of composite data types.

options.c: Statement 1 is true, but Statement 2 is false.
options.d: Statement 1 is false, but Statement 2 is true.

questions.solution: (c) Statement 1 is true, but Statement 2 is false. int and float are primitive types; classes and arrays are composite types.

questions.chapter: Values, Data Types and Operators
questions.question:
Statement 1 : Java is a strongly typed language, ensuring all variables have specific types.
Statement 2 : The type of a variable in Java can change during program execution.

options.c: Statement 1 is true, but Statement 2 is false.
options.d: Statement 1 is false, but Statement 2 is true.

questions.solution: (c) Statement 1 is true, but Statement 2 is false. A variable's declared type is fixed at compile time and cannot change while the program runs.

questions.chapter: Class as the Basis of Computation
questions.question:
Assertion (A) : The new operator in Java allocates memory to an object at runtime.
Reason (R) : The new operator in Java initializes all instance variables to their default values.

options.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
options.b: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
options.c: A is true, but R is false.
options.d: A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution: (b) Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. Both are true: new allocates memory at runtime, and the fresh object's instance variables get default values (0, 0.0, false, null). But giving default values does not explain why memory is allocated at runtime, so R is not the explanation of A. (Corrected: the source key said (a).)

questions.chapter: Encapsulation
questions.question:
Assertion (A) : Access specifiers in Java are used to control the visibility of data members and member functions.
Reason (R) : Protected access specifier in Java makes members visible only within the same class.

options.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
options.b: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
options.c: A is true, but R is false.
options.d: A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution: (c) A is true, but R is false. protected members are visible in the same class, the same package and subclasses; only private restricts access to the same class.

questions.chapter: Values, Data Types and Operators
questions.question: What are the different set of data types available in Java?
questions.solution:
Java has two sets of data types:
(i) Primitive (intrinsic) data types: the eight built-in types byte, short, int, long, float, double, char and boolean.
(ii) Reference (non-primitive / composite) data types: classes, arrays and interfaces (e.g. String, Scanner, int[]); a variable of these types holds a reference to the data.

marking_points.point: Primitive data types named with examples
Reference / non-primitive data types named with examples

questions.chapter: Encapsulation
questions.question: Difference between public and private modifiers for members of a class.
questions.solution:
public: a public member can be accessed from any class, in any package.
private: a private member can be accessed only inside the class in which it is declared.

marking_points.point: public: accessible from any class / anywhere
private: accessible only within its own class

questions.chapter: Values, Data Types and Operators
questions.question: List various reference data types of Java.
questions.solution:
Reference data types in Java are:
(i) Class (e.g. String, Scanner or any user-defined class; its objects are accessed through references)
(ii) Array (e.g. int[], String[])
(iii) Interface

marking_points.point: Class (objects of a class)
Array and interface

questions.chapter: Encapsulation
questions.question: What are the primary access specifiers in Java?
questions.solution:
(i) public: the member is accessible from any class in any package.
(ii) private: the member is accessible only inside the class where it is declared.
(iii) protected: the member is accessible inside its class, by other classes in the same package and by subclasses.
(If no specifier is written, the member has default (package) access: visible only within the same package.)

marking_points.point: public with its scope
private with its scope
protected with its scope

questions.chapter: Class as the Basis of Computation
questions.question: What is the role of the new operator in Java?
questions.solution:
The new operator allocates memory for an object at runtime (dynamically), creates the object by calling the constructor, and returns a reference to it.
Example: Student obj = new Student(); creates a Student object and stores its reference in obj.

marking_points.point: Allocates memory for an object at runtime / creates an instance
Returns the reference, with a correct example

questions.chapter: Class as the Basis of Computation
questions.question: Explain how the objects communicate with each other. Illustrate the concept by taking an example of the objects around you.
questions.solution:
Objects communicate by message passing: one object calls a method of another object and passes it data as arguments; the called object does the work and may return a result.
Example: student A passes the marks of six subjects to student B. B uses its method to calculate the total and percentage and returns the result to A. A and B are the objects, the marks are the arguments of the message, and the percentage-calculating method is the behaviour invoked. In Java this is written as b.percentage(marks...), i.e. message passing = calling a method with arguments.

marking_points.point: Objects communicate by message passing (calling another object's methods)
Data is sent as arguments and a result may be returned
A suitable real-life example clearly mapped to objects, message and method
